items.question: What is a unit fraction?
items.note: The lesson names unit fractions. It does not say what one is.
items.answer: A unit fraction is a fraction that has 1 on top, like 1/4. It means one equal part of a whole. For example, 1/4 is one of four equal parts.

items.question: What does partition mean?
items.note: Partition is named in the first objective and the first activity. It is not defined.
items.answer: Partition means to cut or split something into equal parts. In this lesson, you will partition the number line from 0 to 1 into equal pieces, like cutting it into 4 equal parts to make fourths.

items.question: What is a number line?
items.note: Number line is named. The package never says what one is.
items.answer: A number line is a straight line with numbers placed at equal distances. In this lesson, you use it to show fractions, like marking the point for 1/4 between 0 and 1.

items.question: What is a tick mark?
items.note: Activity 1 tells learners to draw tick marks. It does not say what a tick mark is.
items.answer: A tick mark is a small line you draw on a number line to show where a part or a number goes, like when you split the line from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts, you make tick marks to show each part.

items.question: What does equal parts mean?
items.note: Equal parts is named. The package does not define it.
items.answer: Equal parts means pieces of the number line that are all the same size. In this lesson, you will split the space from 0 to 1 into equal parts, like cutting a bar into 4 identical pieces. Each piece is one unit fraction, such as 1/4.

items.question: What is an interval?
items.note: Interval is named in the first objective. It is not defined.
items.answer: An interval is the space or distance between two points on a number line. In this lesson, we look at the interval from 0 to 1 and split it into equal parts, like cutting a bar into pieces. Each equal part helps us place fractions like 1/4 on the line.

items.question: What is the Malthusian trap?
items.note: Activity 2 names the Malthusian trap. It does not define it.
items.answer: The Malthusian trap is the idea that any rise in income or food supply leads to more people, so output per person gets pulled back down to a bare subsistence level. Because land is limited and food production has diminishing returns, population growth eventually cancels out gains in living standards. In this lesson it is one of the key mechanisms in classical growth theory.

items.question: What is the Solow-Swan model?
items.note: Activity 3 names the model and a numerical example. It does not define the model.
items.answer: The Solow-Swan model, from your teacher's notes, is a way to see how saving, population growth, and technology determine the level of output an economy settles at in the long run. It explains steady-state output, but it still can't fully explain why some countries are richer, leaving a leftover part (total factor productivity) that your lesson points to as a gateway to deeper causes like institutions and geography.

items.question: What are deep determinants of growth?
items.note: The objective and several activities name the phrase. They do not define it.
items.answer: Deep determinants of growth are the underlying factors that explain why some economies grow persistently faster than others: institutions, geography, culture, and openness. They are called 'deep' because they lie beneath immediate inputs like capital and labor and shape how productive those inputs are.

items.question: What is total factor productivity?
items.note: Activity 3 names total factor productivity as what the model leaves out. It does not define it.
items.answer: Total factor productivity is the part of output growth that is not explained by measured inputs like capital and labor—the "residual" in the Solow-Swan model. In this lesson, it is what the model leaves unexplained, and it serves as a gateway to deep determinants such as institutions and geography.

items.question: What is entropy?
items.note: N4 18+: on the subject (thermodynamics), not in the lesson; a general explanation.
items.answer: Entropy is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system. In thermodynamics, it quantifies the amount of energy that is unavailable to do work as energy transforms. The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time.

items.question: How does a refrigerator move heat from cold to hot?
items.note: N4 18+: refrigeration cycles are thermodynamics but not in this lesson.
items.answer: A refrigerator uses external work (from a compressor) to force heat to flow from a cold interior to a warmer room. The working fluid absorbs heat at low temperature and pressure, is compressed to high pressure and temperature, then releases heat to the surroundings and expands to repeat the cycle. This input of work makes the non-spontaneous transfer possible, even though heat naturally moves from hot to cold.

items.question: What is the difference between an isothermal and an adiabatic process?
items.note: N4 18+: process types are on the subject, not in the lesson.
items.answer: An isothermal process happens at constant temperature, so heat is exchanged with the surroundings to keep the temperature steady. An adiabatic process has no heat transfer at all, so any work done changes the internal energy and therefore the temperature.

items.question: Why can no heat engine be 100% efficient?
items.note: N4 18+: second-law limit; on the subject, not in the lesson.
items.answer: A heat engine must reject some heat to a cold reservoir because energy cannot be completely converted to work in a cyclic process (second law of thermodynamics). Even an ideal engine (Carnot) has an efficiency less than 100% unless the cold reservoir is at absolute zero, which is impossible. So all real engines lose some heat to the surroundings.

items.question: What does enthalpy mean?
items.note: N4 18+: enthalpy is not named by the lesson; a general explanation.
items.answer: Enthalpy (H) is a thermodynamic property defined as the internal energy of a system plus the product of its pressure and volume (H = U + PV). It is useful because for a constant-pressure process, the change in enthalpy equals the heat added or removed. In this lesson, you use the first law for a closed system and boundary work at constant pressure, but enthalpy itself is not defined in the course material.
